claim: Efficient neural processing depends on regulating responses through suppression and facilitation of neural activity.
source: Efficient neural processing depends on regulating responses through suppression and facilitation of neural activity.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the study's context.

claim: Both suppression and facilitation can emerge from a single computational principle – divisive normalization.
source: both suppression and facilitation can emerge from a single, computational principle – divisive normalization; there is no need to invoke separate neural mechanisms
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2 and described in the Results section.

claim: Neural suppression and facilitation in the motion-selective area MT mirror perception.
source: neural suppression and facilitation in the motion-selective area MT mirror perception
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data presented in Figure 3 showing correspondence between neural responses in hMT+ and behavioral performance.

claim: Strong suppression occurs in earlier visual areas.
source: strong suppression also occurs in earlier visual areas
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data from EVC shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Suppression is not primarily driven by GABA-mediated inhibition.
source: suppression is not primarily driven by GABA-mediated inhibition
evidence: This is supported by both the lorazepam pharmacology experiment (Figure 4) and MRS measurements (Figure 5) showing no direct link between GABA and spatial suppression.

claim: Spatial suppression paradigms should not be used to infer neural inhibition.
source: while commonly used spatial suppression paradigms may provide insight into neural response magnitudes in visual areas, they should not be used to infer neural inhibition
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined results of pharmacology and MRS experiments showing no direct relationship between GABA and spatial suppression.

claim: Processes that regulate the level of activity within neural circuits play a critical role in information processing by enabling efficient coding.
source: Processes that regulate the level of activity within neural circuits (Carandini and Heeger, 2012) are thought to play a critical role in information processing by enabling efficient coding (Vinje and Gallant, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Both suppression and facilitation of neural responses emerge in the visual system via spatial context effects.
source: Both suppression and facilitation of neural responses are well-known to emerge in the visual system via spatial context effects, and have a variety of perceptual consequences.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the subsequent description of spatial suppression and summation effects.

claim: More time is needed to discriminate the direction of motion of a large high-contrast grating compared to one that is small.
source: Specifically, more time is needed to discriminate the direction of motion of a large high-contrast grating compared to one that is small.
evidence: This is supported by the psychophysical data presented in Figure 2C and is a well-established phenomenon in the literature (Tadin et al., 2003; Tadin, 2015).

claim: Spatial suppression has been suggested to reflect GABAergic inhibitory interactions from extra-classical receptive field surrounds.
source: This seemingly paradoxical effect is referred to as spatial suppression and has been suggested to reflect GABAergic inhibitory interactions from extra-classical receptive field (RF) surrounds (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a commonly held assumption in the field that the study aims to test, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Less time is needed to discriminate motion direction for a large compared to small stimulus at low contrast.
source: The effect of size on duration thresholds is reversed for a low-contrast stimulus – less time is needed to discriminate motion direction for a large compared to small stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by psychophysical data in Figure 2C and established literature.

claim: Spatial summation has been suggested to reflect neural enhancement from RF surrounds and/or an enlargement of RFs at low contrast.
source: This facilitation of behavior is referred to as spatial summation and has been suggested to reflect neural enhancement from RF surrounds (e.g. glutamatergic excitation) and/or an enlargement of RFs at low contrast (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a commonly held assumption illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The spatial suppression paradigm has been applied to the study of schizophrenia.
source: This paradigm has been applied to the study of multiple clinical phenomena including schizophrenia (Tadin et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The spatial suppression paradigm has been applied to the study of major depressive disorder.
source: major depressive disorder (Golomb et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The spatial suppression paradigm has been applied to the study of migraine.
source: migraine (Battista et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The spatial suppression paradigm has been applied to the study of autism spectrum disorder.
source: autism spectrum disorder (Foss-Feig et al., 2013; Rosenberg et al., 2015; Sysoeva et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The spatial suppression paradigm has been applied to the study of epilepsy.
source: epilepsy (Yazdani et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The spatial suppression paradigm has been applied to the study of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Alzheimer's disease (Zhuang et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The spatial suppression paradigm has been applied to the study of normal aging.
source: normal aging (Betts et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The spatial suppression paradigm has been applied to the study of ethanol intoxication.
source: ethanol intoxication (Read et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: It has been assumed that spatial suppression and summation reflect distinct neural mechanisms that rely on inhibitory and excitatory processes, respectively.
source: Generally, it has been assumed that spatial suppression and summation reflect distinct neural mechanisms that rely on inhibitory and excitatory processes, respectively (Ma et al., 2010; Yoon et al., 2010; Cook et al., 2016; Haider et al., 2010; Adesnik et al., 2012; Nienborg et al., 2013; but see [Ozeki et al., 2004; Ozeki et al., 2009; Shushruth et al., 2012; Sato et al., 2016; Liu and Pack, 2014)
evidence: This is a commonly held assumption in the field, supported by multiple citations, which the study aims to challenge.

claim: Spatial suppression and summation are thought to occur within brain regions involved in visual motion processing, particularly area MT.
source: within brain regions involved in visual motion processing (particularly area MT)
evidence: This is a commonly held assumption based on previous literature.

claim: Neural responses in human MT complex indexed with fMRI correspond well with the measured perceptual effect.
source: While neural responses in human MT complex (hMT+) indexed with fMRI correspond well with the measured perceptual effect
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data presented in Figure 3C showing both suppression and summation in hMT+.

claim: It is possible that hMT+ 'inherits' suppression from earlier stages of processing.
source: there is substantial suppression in earlier visual areas; thus, it is possible that hMT+ 'inherits' suppression from earlier stages of processing
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of strong suppression in EVC (Figure 3B) and the known connectivity between visual areas.

claim: Two separate methodologies fail to show a direct link between spatial suppression and the strength of neural inhibition.
source: Two separate methodologies – magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) and pharmacological potentiation of GABAA receptors – fail to show a direct link between spatial suppression and the strength of neural inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by the lorazepam experiment (Figure 4) and MRS measurements (Figure 5).

claim: Inhibition plays a role in motion perception.
source: Although we find that inhibition plays a role in motion perception
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of lorazepam on motion discrimination thresholds (Figure 4).

claim: Increases in duration threshold as a function of stimulus size should not be taken as an index of inhibitory processing.
source: increases in duration threshold as a function of stimulus size should not be taken as an index of inhibitory processing
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined results showing no direct relationship between GABA and spatial suppression.

claim: A single computational principle – divisive normalization – can account for spatial context effects.
source: our results suggest that a single computational principle – divisive normalization – can account for spatial context effects
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results presented in Figure 2.

claim: Suppressive context effects are not driven by neural inhibition.
source: suppressive context effects are not driven by neural inhibition
evidence: This is supported by the lorazepam and MRS experiments showing no direct link between GABA and suppression.

claim: Motion duration thresholds were measured for 10 subjects in six different stimulus conditions.
source: To quantify spatial suppression and summation psychophysically, we measured motion duration thresholds (see Materials and methods) for 10 subjects in each of six different stimulus conditions
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample size.

claim: Stimuli were sinusoidal luminance gratings at three different sizes and two different contrasts.
source: with sinusoidal luminance gratings at three different sizes (small [s], medium [m], and big [b]; diameter = 1, 2 and 12°, respectively) and two different contrasts (low = 3%; high = 98%; Figure 2A–C)
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters used in the experiment, illustrated in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Negative size index values indicate more time was needed for motion discrimination with larger stimuli (spatial suppression).
source: Negative SI values indicate more time was needed for motion discrimination with larger stimuli (spatial suppression)
evidence: This defines the size index metric used to quantify spatial suppression.

claim: Positive size index values indicate shorter durations for larger stimuli (spatial summation).
source: while positive values indicate shorter durations for larger stimuli (spatial summation)
evidence: This defines the size index metric used to quantify spatial summation.

claim: Size indices depended on both size and contrast.
source: As expected (Tadin et al., 2003; Tadin, 2015), SIs depended on both size and contrast (F2,9 = 27.3, p=4 × 10−6)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the psychophysical data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Spatial suppression was observed at high contrast.
source: with spatial suppression observed at high contrast
evidence: This is shown in the psychophysical data in Figure 2D.

claim: Spatial summation was observed at low contrast.
source: and spatial summation at low contrast (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is shown in the psychophysical data in Figure 2D.

claim: The divisive normalization model describes the response (R) to a visual stimulus in terms of an excitatory drive term (E) divided by the sum of a suppressive drive term (S) plus a semi-saturation constant (σ).
source: This model describes the response (R) to a visual stimulus in terms of an excitatory drive term (E; reflecting the strength of the input, that is, stimulus contrast), divided by the sum of a suppressive drive term (S; also depends on input strength but is spatially broader; Figure 2E) plus a small number known as the semi-saturation constant (σ; controls response sensitivity; see Materials and methods and Appendix 1 for further model details).
evidence: This explains the components of the divisive normalization model, illustrated in Figure 2E.

claim: The divisive normalization model has been used to describe how normalization may contribute to a wide range of neural functions.
source: This model has been used previously to describe how normalization may contribute to a wide range of neural functions, from early visual processing and attention to olfaction and decision making (Carandini and Heeger, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comprehensive review.

claim: A good qualitative match between psychophysical motion discrimination data and the model predictions was obtained by assuming that the amount of time required for motion discrimination is inversely related to the peak modeled response.
source: We found that a good qualitative match between our psychophysical motion discrimination data and the model predictions (Figure 2F–H) could be obtained by assuming that the amount of time required for motion discrimination is inversely related to the peak modeled response (see Materials and methods; Equation 3).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach and its success in matching the data, shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: At high contrast, as stimulus size grows the modeled suppressive drive increases relative to the excitatory drive, so the predicted response decreases.
source: At high contrast, as stimulus size grows the modeled suppressive drive increases relative to the excitatory drive, so the predicted response decreases (i.e. spatial suppression; red curve in Figure 2F).
evidence: This explains the model's prediction for high-contrast stimuli, illustrated in Figure 2F.

claim: For low contrasts and small sizes, the suppressive drive is relatively weak compared to the semi-saturation constant, so the response to low-contrast stimuli increases with stimulus size until the suppressive drive is relatively larger than the semi-saturation constant.
source: For low contrasts and small sizes, the suppressive drive is relatively weak compared to the semi-saturation constant (σ), so the response to low-contrast stimuli increases with stimulus size until the suppressive drive is relatively larger than σ (i.e. spatial summation; blue curve in Figure 2F).
evidence: This explains the model's prediction for low-contrast stimuli, illustrated in Figure 2F.

claim: The parameters that determine spatial selectivity do not vary with stimulus contrast in the model.
source: Note that the parameters that determine spatial selectivity (i.e. model receptive field size) do not vary with stimulus contrast.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model implementation.

claim: Within the computational framework of the model, spatial suppression vs. summation depends on the strength of the suppressive drive relative to σ at a given stimulus contrast.
source: Instead, within the computational framework of this model, spatial suppression vs. summation depends on the strength of the suppressive drive relative to σ at a given stimulus contrast.
evidence: This explains the mechanism by which the model produces both suppression and summation.

claim: In macaque visual cortex, the peak neural response is often observed at larger sizes for lower contrast stimuli.
source: In macaque visual cortex, the peak neural response is likewise often observed at larger sizes for lower contrast stimuli (Angelucci and Bressloff, 2006; Pack et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in animal models.

claim: The complex interplay between stimulus contrast and size that results in spatial suppression and summation during motion perception may be accounted for by a simple divisive normalization rule.
source: Thus, the complex interplay between stimulus contrast and size that results in spatial suppression and summation during motion perception may be accounted for by a simple divisive normalization rule – it is not necessary to invoke distinct neural mechanisms to explain both phenomena.
evidence: This is a key conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: FMRI responses to low- and high-contrast moving gratings at different sizes were measured with the same 10 subjects from the psychophysical experiment.
source: To test this hypothesis directly in human visual cortex, we measured fMRI responses to low- and high-contrast moving gratings at different sizes with the same 10 subjects from the psychophysical experiment above.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the fMRI study.

claim: Responses were reported from two areas: early visual cortex (EVC) and human MT complex (hMT+).
source: We report the responses from two areas: (1) early visual cortex (EVC; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) which was located at the foveal confluence of areas V1, V2, and V3, near the occipital pole and (2) human MT complex (hMT+; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes the regions of interest analyzed in the fMRI study.

claim: Sub-regions-of-interest were defined corresponding to cortical areas that selectively respond to the smallest stimulus size.
source: For both EVC and hMT+, we used an independent localizer scan to define sub regions-of-interest (sub-ROIs) corresponding to cortical areas that selectively respond to the smallest stimulus size (Olman et al., 2007; Schallmo et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the method for defining ROIs in the fMRI analysis.

claim: During a single experimental scan, two stimulus sizes were presented in alternating 10 s blocks.
source: During a single experimental scan, two stimulus sizes were presented in alternating 10 s blocks: either small and medium or small and big.
evidence: This describes the fMRI experimental design, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The sub-ROIs were constantly stimulated during the scan.
source: Thus, the sub-ROIs – defined by the smallest stimulus size – were constantly stimulated during the scan.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: The response during the small block served as a baseline for the larger block.
source: This method allowed us to directly compare the relative fMRI responses to larger vs. smaller stimuli (i.e. the response during the small block served as a baseline for the larger block, which was the condition of interest).
evidence: This describes the analysis approach for the fMRI data.

claim: If responses in EVC and hMT+ sub-ROIs did not change between the small and larger stimulus blocks, this would indicate no influence of surrounding regions on response magnitude.
source: If responses in EVC and hMT+ sub-ROIs did not change between the small and larger stimulus blocks (the null hypothesis), this would indicate no influence of surrounding regions on response magnitude.
evidence: This states the null hypothesis for the fMRI experiment.

claim: Increased fMRI responses would reflect spatial summation.
source: Increased responses would reflect spatial summation
evidence: This defines the interpretation of increased fMRI responses.

claim: Spatial suppression would yield decreased fMRI responses.
source: while spatial suppression would yield response decreases
evidence: This defines the interpretation of decreased fMRI responses.

claim: In EVC, there was no evidence for neural summation at low contrast.
source: In EVC, there was no evidence for neural summation at low contrast; responses did not change (small-to-medium [s-m]; Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) or decreased slightly (s-b) when low-contrast stimuli became larger.
evidence: This is shown in the fMRI data from EVC in Figure 3B.

claim: At high contrast, suppression was observed in EVC.
source: However, at high contrast, suppression was observed in EVC (F1,9 = 18.0, p=0.002) and was particularly strong in the small-to-big condition.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the fMRI data from EVC shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In hMT+, there was evidence for both neural summation and suppression at low and high contrast, respectively.
source: In hMT+, there was evidence for both neural summation and suppression at low and high contrast, respectively.
evidence: This is shown in the fMRI data from hMT+ in Figure 3C.

claim: FMRI responses in hMT+ increased with stimulus size at low contrast.
source: FMRI responses in hMT+ increased with stimulus size at low contrast (consistent with neural summation)
evidence: This is shown in the fMRI data in Figure 3C.

claim: FMRI responses in hMT+ decreased with stimulus size at high contrast.
source: and decreased at high contrast (consistent with neural suppression; Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; F1,7 = 9.0, p=0.020)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the fMRI data from hMT+ shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The pattern of fMRI responses in hMT+ is a better match to the spatial summation and suppression observed using psychophysics, as compared to EVC.
source: This pattern of fMRI responses is a better match to the spatial summation and suppression observed using psychophysics (from Figure 2D), as compared to EVC which did not show any summation.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the fMRI results (Figure 3) with the psychophysical results (Figure 2D).

claim: The overall smaller fMRI response modulation in hMT+ vs. EVC was expected due to larger receptive fields in hMT+.
source: The overall smaller fMRI response modulation in hMT+ vs. EVC was expected due to larger receptive fields in hMT+ (Amano et al., 2009), which reduce the retinotopic selectivity of the hemodynamic response within this ROI.
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of receptive fields in hMT+, supported by citation.

claim: The fMRI results are consistent with the proposal that increased and decreased neural activity within hMT+ contributes to spatial summation and suppression during motion perception.
source: These fMRI results are consistent with the proposal that increased and decreased neural activity within hMT+ contributes to spatial summation and suppression (respectively) during motion perception (Liu et al., 2016; Tadin, 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the correspondence between fMRI responses in hMT+ and psychophysical performance, supported by citations.

claim: Observing both suppression and summation together within a single region is consistent with the framework of the normalization model.
source: Observing both suppression and summation together within a single region is consistent with the framework of the normalization model (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Suppression is clearly strong within earlier visual areas (EVC), even for low-contrast stimuli.
source: In addition, it should be emphasized that suppression is clearly strong within earlier visual areas (EVC), even for low-contrast stimuli.
evidence: This is shown in the fMRI data from EVC in Figure 3B.

claim: The a priori hypothesis was that if suppression depends on GABA-mediated inhibition, increases in GABA signaling should correspond with increased duration thresholds specifically for big stimuli.
source: Our a priori hypothesis was that if suppression depends on GABA-mediated inhibition, increases in GABA signaling (either pharmacological or by natural variation in GABA concentration across individuals) should correspond with increased duration thresholds specifically for big stimuli – where suppression is greatest.
evidence: This states the hypothesis being tested in the lorazepam and MRS experiments.

claim: Lorazepam acts as a positive allosteric modulator at the GABAA receptor.
source: We first examined the effect of potentiating inhibition through administration of the benzodiazepine drug lorazepam, which acts as a positive allosteric modulator at the GABAA receptor (Haefely, 1983).
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Lorazepam causes chloride channels to open more readily in response to GABA binding, which yields greater inhibition of neural action potentials.
source: This compound causes chloride channels to open more readily in response to GABA binding, which yields greater inhibition of neural action potentials.
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge about the mechanism of lorazepam.

claim: In a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover experiment, 15 subjects received either a 1.5 mg dose of lorazepam or placebo during separate experimental sessions on different days.
source: In a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover experiment, 15 subjects received either a 1.5 mg dose of lorazepam or placebo during separate experimental sessions on different days (order randomized and counter-balanced across subjects).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the lorazepam study.

claim: Increasing inhibition via lorazepam did not lead to stronger suppression.
source: We found that increasing inhibition via lorazepam did not lead to stronger suppression – in fact, we observed weaker spatial suppression (SIs were less negative overall) under lorazepam vs. placebo (Figure 4C; F1,14 = 6.51, p=0.023).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the lorazepam data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Lorazepam increased thresholds to some extent across all conditions.
source: Rather than increasing suppression, we found that lorazepam affected motion discrimination in two ways: first, lorazepam increased thresholds to some extent across all conditions (F1,14 = 9.83, p=0.007).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the lorazepam data.

claim: The effect of lorazepam was stronger for smaller stimuli at both low and high contrast.
source: More importantly, the effect of lorazepam (drug minus placebo) was stronger for smaller stimuli (Figure 4D; F1,14 = 6.91, p=0.020) at both low and high contrast.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the lorazepam data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: By increasing thresholds for smaller stimuli, lorazepam effectively weakened spatial suppression.
source: By increasing thresholds for smaller stimuli, lorazepam effectively weakened spatial suppression (i.e. reduced the difference in thresholds between small and larger stimuli).
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Potentiating inhibition at the GABAA receptor via lorazepam decreased, rather than increased spatial suppression.
source: Thus, we found that potentiating inhibition at the GABAA receptor via lorazepam decreased, rather than increased spatial suppression in this paradigm.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the lorazepam experiment.

claim: The lorazepam result is not consistent with the idea that spatial suppression is directly mediated by neural inhibition.
source: This result is not consistent with the idea that spatial suppression is directly mediated by neural inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the unexpected effect of lorazepam on spatial suppression.

claim: The concentration of GABA+ was quantified within specific regions of visual cortex using MRS.
source: To further examine the relationship between spatial suppression and inhibition, we measured the concentration of GABA+ (GABA plus co-edited macromolecules) within specific regions of visual cortex using MRS.
evidence: This describes the MRS methodology.

claim: GABA+ was quantified within moderately sized voxels centered on functionally identified hMT+, anatomically identified EVC, and a control voxel in anatomically identified parietal cortex.
source: GABA+ was quantified within moderately sized voxels (27 cm3) centered on functionally identified hMT+ (left and right hemispheres measured in separate scans and averaged; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), anatomically identified EVC (average of 2 measurements in the same region; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), and a control voxel in anatomically identified parietal cortex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes the MRS voxel locations, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: MRS data were acquired at rest.
source: MRS data were acquired at rest (i.e. subjects were not asked to perform a specific task).
evidence: This describes the MRS acquisition protocol.

claim: The same subjects also participated in separate psychophysical and fMRI experiments to measure spatial suppression.
source: The same subjects also participated in separate psychophysical and fMRI experiments to measure spatial suppression, comparable to those described above (N = 22 complete data sets).
evidence: This describes the experimental design linking MRS with behavioral and fMRI measures.

claim: MRS measurements of GABA+ are thought to reflect stable, individual differences in the baseline concentration of this neurotransmitter.
source: Unlike manipulating GABA pharmacologically, MRS measurements of GABA+ are thought to reflect stable, individual differences in the baseline concentration of this neurotransmitter (Evans et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on the stability of MRS measurements.

claim: The strength of spatial suppression did not depend on the concentration of GABA+ in hMT+.
source: Behaviorally, the strength of spatial suppression did not depend on the concentration of GABA+ in hMT+; no significant correlations were found between hMT+ GABA+ and SIs (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–F; all |r20-25|<0.32, uncorrected p-values>0.14).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A-F.

claim: There were no significant associations between fMRI measurements of spatial suppression in hMT+ and the concentration of GABA+ in this region.
source: Further, there were no significant associations between fMRI measurements of spatial suppression in hMT+ and the concentration of GABA+ in this region (Figure 5—figure supplement 3G–H; |r19| < 0.29, uncorrected p-values>0.20).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3G-H.

claim: More GABA+ in hMT+ correlated with overall better psychophysical performance during motion direction discrimination.
source: Instead, we made the surprising observation that more GABA+ in hMT+ correlated with overall better psychophysical performance (lower thresholds on average) during motion direction discrimination (Figure 5D; r20 = −0.46, p=0.030, uncorrected).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: More GABA in hMT+ is associated with better motion discrimination in general but not with the strength of spatial suppression.
source: These results suggest that more GABA in hMT+ is associated with better motion discrimination in general but not with the strength of spatial suppression.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of correlations between GABA+ in hMT+ and behavioral measures.

claim: When examining GABA+ measured within other areas (EVC or parietal cortex), no significant relationships were found with spatial suppression or overall psychophysical thresholds.
source: When examining GABA+ measured within other areas (EVC or parietal cortex), no significant relationships were found with spatial suppression or overall psychophysical thresholds, nor did GABA+ correlate significantly with spatial suppression measured in EVC using fMRI (all |r19-25|<0.28, uncorrected p-values>0.21; Figure 5—figure supplement 4 and Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 and Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: The relationship between motion discrimination performance and GABA+ is specific to hMT+, and not a more general phenomenon.
source: These findings suggest that the relationship between motion discrimination performance and GABA+ is specific to hMT+, and not a more general (e.g. brain-wide) phenomenon.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlations in other brain regions.

claim: The spectroscopy results show no evidence for the predicted association between stronger spatial suppression and greater GABA in visual cortex.
source: Together, our spectroscopy results show no evidence for the predicted association between stronger spatial suppression and greater GABA in visual cortex, as indexed by MRS.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the MRS experiment.

claim: Higher GABA+ in hMT+ was associated with better motion discrimination performance overall.
source: Instead, higher GABA+ in hMT+ was associated with better motion discrimination performance overall.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The effect of lorazepam on motion discrimination differs from the effect of individual differences in GABA+ measured with MRS.
source: While this result differs from the effect of lorazepam on motion discrimination described above, we note that MRS reflects individual differences in GABA+ within visual brain areas that are (presumably) at homeostasis, whereas the effects of lorazepam can be attributed to a transient pharmacological strengthening of inhibition specific to the GABAA receptor class.
evidence: This is inferred from the different nature of the two manipulations.

claim: This study did not find a major role for GABA in determining the strength of spatial suppression.
source: This study examined a number of common assumptions about the neural processes underlying spatial suppression and summation during motion perception. Although this paradigm has been posited as a behavioral index for inhibition, we did not find a major role for GABA in determining the strength of spatial suppression.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the combined lorazepam and MRS experiments.

claim: Some reports suggest that GABAergic inhibition plays a direct role in surround suppression within visual cortex.
source: Some reports suggest that GABAergic inhibition plays a direct role in surround suppression within visual cortex (Ma et al., 2010; Haider et al., 2010; Adesnik et al., 2012; Nienborg et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in animal models.

claim: Other reports have indicated that surround suppression occurs via withdrawal of excitation, which may be balanced by reduced inhibition.
source: while others have indicated that this suppression occurs via withdrawal of excitation (Ozeki et al., 2004; Ozeki et al., 2009; Shushruth et al., 2012; Sato et al., 2016), which may be balanced by reduced inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in animal models.

claim: The findings seem more consistent with the withdrawal of excitation as a mechanism for spatial suppression.
source: Nevertheless, our findings seem more consistent with the withdrawal of excitation as a mechanism for spatial suppression.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of evidence for a direct role of GABA in spatial suppression.

claim: Blocking GABA in macaque MT had no effect on spatial suppression.
source: This agrees with an earlier observation that blocking GABA in macaque MT had no effect on spatial suppression (Liu and Pack, 2014) (see also [Katzner et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in animal models.

claim: The MRS findings appear to conflict with reports that greater mid-occipital GABA was associated with stronger surround suppression during contrast perception.
source: However, our MRS findings appear to conflict with reports that greater mid-occipital GABA was associated with stronger surround suppression during contrast perception (Yoon et al., 2010; Cook et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the current results with previous findings, supported by citations.

claim: The discrepancy between the current findings and previous reports may be related to the methods for quantifying suppression, and/or differences in the role of inhibition during perception of contrast and motion.
source: This discrepancy may be related to the methods for quantifying suppression, and/or differences in the role of inhibition during perception of contrast and motion.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for the discrepancy with previous findings.

claim: A reduction in both input and output gain yields predicted thresholds that mirror the observed effects of lorazepam.
source: Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D shows how a reduction in both input (i.e. contrast) and output (i.e. response) gain yields predicted thresholds that mirror the observed effects of lorazepam (compare with Figure 4A–D; also see Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is shown in the modeling results in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Higher thresholds for smaller stimuli following lorazepam may be accounted for in the normalization model by reducing the strength of the input.
source: Specifically, higher thresholds for smaller stimuli following lorazepam may be accounted for in the normalization model by reducing the strength of the input (i.e. reduced contrast gain).
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results.

claim: Lowering contrast gain raised the predicted thresholds for small stimuli but had little effect when stimuli were large.
source: Lowering contrast gain raised the predicted thresholds for small stimuli but had little effect when stimuli were large.
evidence: This is shown in the modeling results.

claim: The effect of lorazepam in reducing spatial suppression may be consistent with reduced contrast gain within brain regions relevant to motion perception.
source: We therefore speculate that the effect of lorazepam in reducing spatial suppression may be consistent with reduced contrast gain within brain regions relevant to motion perception (e.g. MT).
evidence: This is speculation based on the modeling results.

claim: It may be expected that potentiating inhibition at the GABAA receptor would reduce neural responsiveness overall.
source: From previous work that manipulated GABAA receptor function in animal models (Katzner et al., 2011; Thiele et al., 2004), it may be expected that potentiating inhibition at this receptor would reduce neural responsiveness overall (i.e. lower response gain).
evidence: This is inferred from previous work in animal models, supported by citations.

claim: Lorazepam raised motion discrimination thresholds across conditions, an effect that is consistent with overall lower neural responses.
source: Beyond increasing thresholds for small stimuli, lorazepam also raised motion discrimination thresholds across conditions (Figure 4D), an effect that is consistent with overall lower neural responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Benzodiazepine administration generally reduces visual performance.
source: This is also consistent with earlier behavioral studies showing that benzodiazepine administration generally reduces visual performance (van Loon et al., 2012; Giersch and Herzog, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: The observed effects of lorazepam were specific to threshold-level motion discrimination, especially for smaller stimuli.
source: However, we note that the observed effects of lorazepam were specific to threshold-level motion discrimination (especially for smaller stimuli); catch trial performance was not affected (see Materials and methods), which argues against more general pharmacological effects (e.g. fatigue).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of catch trial performance.

claim: The effect of lorazepam during motion discrimination may be consistent with weaker contrast gain and perhaps also lower response gain.
source: In summary, while the effect of lorazepam during motion discrimination may be consistent with weaker contrast gain (and perhaps also lower response gain), our findings do not support the idea that spatial suppression is directly mediated by inhibition.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the lorazepam experiment and modeling.

claim: Higher baseline GABA is associated with better, rather than suppressed motion perception.
source: We additionally showed that higher baseline GABA (as measured by MRS) is associated with better, rather than suppressed motion perception.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The correlation between higher GABA+ in hMT+ and better motion discrimination was unexpected.
source: Because this correlation was unexpected, and no statistical correction for multiple comparisons was performed, this result should be interpreted with caution.
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of the correlation.

claim: If more baseline GABA lowers the behavioral response criterion, possibly by improving neural signal-to-noise, then we would expect better performance with higher GABA in hMT+.
source: Alternatively, if more baseline GABA lowers the behavioral response criterion (without necessarily changing the neural response), possibly by improving neural signal-to-noise (Leventhal et al., 2003; Edden et al., 2009; Puts et al., 2011), then we would expect better performance with higher GABA in hMT+.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: Within the model, reducing the response criterion has the same effect on the predicted threshold as an increased neural response.
source: Indeed, within our model (Equation 3), reducing the response criterion has the same effect on the predicted threshold as an increased neural response.
evidence: This is inferred from the mathematical structure of the model.

claim: Changing the criterion has no effect on the strength of spatial suppression predicted by the model.
source: Note that changing the criterion has no effect on the strength of spatial suppression predicted by the model (Figure 5—figure supplement 6C).
evidence: This is shown in the modeling results in Figure 5—figure supplement 6C.

claim: A lower response criterion indicates that less sensory evidence is used to reach the same decision.
source: In terms of the motion discrimination task, a lower response criterion indicates that less sensory evidence (i.e. shorter stimulus duration) is used to reach the same decision (i.e. left- vs. right-ward motion) (Huk and Shadlen, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about decision-making, supported by citation.

claim: Lower response criteria with higher baseline GABA may plausibly account for the MRS data.
source: Thus, lower response criteria with higher baseline GABA may plausibly account for our MRS data.
evidence: This is speculation based on the modeling results.

claim: The MRS data contradict the notion that GABAergic inhibition directly determines the strength of spatial suppression.
source: As with our experiment using lorazepam, these MRS data contradict the notion that GABAergic inhibition directly determines the strength of spatial suppression.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the MRS experiment.

claim: The assumption of a direct link between spatial suppression and inhibition is invalid.
source: Altogether, our findings suggest that the assumption of a direct link between spatial suppression and inhibition is invalid.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the combined results of the study.

claim: The normalization model is a model for early visual processing in which a neuron's response is suppressed by the summed response of its neighbors.
source: We considered whether spatial suppression and summation might be described in terms of a single computation – divisive normalization – a model for early visual processing in which a neuron's response is suppressed (divided) by the summed response of its neighbors (Heeger, 1992; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the normalization model, supported by citations.

claim: Rosenberg and colleagues used weaker normalization to explain superior motion discrimination performance in autism spectrum disorder.
source: We are not the first to suggest that the normalization model may account for these phenomena; Rosenberg and colleagues (Rosenberg et al., 2015) used weaker normalization to explain superior motion discrimination performance in autism spectrum disorder (Foss-Feig et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: This study provides the first direct application of the normalization model to this paradigm in typically developing individuals under a variety of experimental conditions.
source: Our study provides the first direct application of this model to this paradigm in typically developing individuals under a variety of experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study.

claim: Earlier work has modeled spatial suppression and summation in terms of other divisive or subtractive computations.
source: While it is perhaps not surprising that this model performs well in this context (Carandini and Heeger, 2012), earlier work has modeled spatial suppression and summation in terms of other divisive (Betts et al., 2012) or subtractive (Tadin and Lappin, 2005) computations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claim: Earlier models have treated 'excitatory' and 'suppressive' mechanisms separately.
source: Generally, these earlier models have treated 'excitatory' and 'suppressive' mechanisms separately (e.g. different contrast sensitivity).
evidence: This is inferred from the description of previous modeling approaches.

claim: The normalization model provides a simpler account, wherein the suppressive drive is essentially the same as the excitatory drive, only broader in space and orientation.
source: The normalization model (Reynolds and Heeger, 2009) used here provides a simpler account, wherein the suppressive drive is essentially the same as the excitatory drive, only broader in space and orientation (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the normalization model used in the study.

claim: The normalization model is sufficient to explain the complex interplay between stimulus size and contrast that produces psychophysical or neural suppression and summation.
source: We found that this normalization model is sufficient to explain the complex interplay between stimulus size and contrast that produces psychophysical (or neural) suppression and summation.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the modeling work.

claim: The normalization framework appears more parsimonious than positing separate mechanisms operating at different stimulus contrasts.
source: This framework appears more parsimonious than positing separate mechanisms (neural or computational) operating at different stimulus contrasts to produce suppression and summation.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the parsimony of the normalization model.

claim: Normalization can describe spatial suppression and summation under a variety of different experimental conditions.
source: Our modeling work shows that normalization can describe spatial suppression and summation under a variety of different experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results across different experiments.

claim: There was good agreement between the predicted model response, psychophysics, and the fMRI response in hMT+.
source: We found good agreement between the predicted model response (Figure 2G and H), psychophysics (Figure 2C and D), and the fMRI response in hMT+ (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown by comparing the results across Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Both suppression and summation were observed in the fMRI response from a sub-region of hMT+ representing the stimulus center.
source: That both suppression and summation were observed in the fMRI response from a sub-region of hMT+ representing the stimulus center indicates that these two effects are co-localized in cortex
evidence: This is inferred from the fMRI results in Figure 3C.

claim: Suppression and summation could plausibly occur within a single neural population.
source: and both could plausibly occur within a single neural population (Pack et al., 2005), which is consistent with the proposed model framework.
evidence: This is inferred from the fMRI results and supported by citation.

claim: The way in which spatial suppression was affected by lorazepam can be explained in terms of the normalization model.
source: Further, the way in which spatial suppression was affected by lorazepam (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D), but not baseline GABA in hMT+ (Figure 5—figure supplement 6A–C), can be explained in terms of the normalization model (Appendix 1-Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in the modeling results in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: The lorazepam data were described by an exponential reduction of contrast gain.
source: It is worth noting that the lorazepam data were described by an exponential reduction of contrast gain, which we speculate may reflect the compounded reduction of neural responses across multiple stages of visual processing (e.g. retina, lateral geniculate nucleus, visual cortex) due to systemic potentiation of inhibition at the GABAA receptor.
evidence: This is speculation based on the modeling approach.

claim: Recent work has suggested some limitations for describing spatial suppression in terms of normalization.
source: Although recent work has suggested some limitations for describing spatial suppression in terms of normalization (Heeger et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: The normalization model framework is sufficiently general to describe the suppression effect across different experiments.
source: we find that this model framework is sufficiently general to describe the suppression effect across our different experiments.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling work across multiple experiments.

claim: FMRI responses in hMT+ showed better agreement with spatial suppression and summation measured psychophysically, as compared with the responses in EVC.
source: Our results generally supported this hypothesis; fMRI responses in hMT+ showed better agreement with spatial suppression and summation measured psychophysically, as compared with the responses in EVC (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is shown by comparing the fMRI results in Figure 3B and C with the psychophysical results.

claim: Better motion discrimination across individuals was predicted by higher GABA+ in hMT+ but not in EVC.
source: Further, better motion discrimination across individuals was predicted by higher GABA+ in hMT+ (Figure 5D), but not in EVC (Figure 5—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is shown by comparing the correlations in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 4D.

claim: The idea that spatial suppression during perception is driven by surround suppression within MT is consistent with recent work in primate models.
source: The idea that spatial suppression during perception is driven (at least in part) by surround suppression within MT is consistent with recent work in primate models (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work in animal models.

claim: For many neurons in primate MT, the presence of stimuli within the extra-classical receptive field surround suppresses or enhances the response to stimuli within the receptive field center.
source: For many neurons in primate MT, the presence of stimuli within the extra-classical receptive field surround suppresses (or enhances) the response to stimuli within the receptive field center (Liu et al., 2016; Pack et al., 2005; Born and Tootell, 1992; Born, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge from animal studies, supported by citations.

claim: The proposed link between perceptual suppression and neural suppression in MT has received support from studies in humans.
source: The proposed link between perceptual suppression and neural suppression in MT has received further (if limited) support from studies in humans (Turkozer et al., 2016; Tadin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human studies.

claim: The findings extend the link between neural processing in hMT+ and motion discrimination performance in human subjects.
source: Using fMRI, MRS, and modeling, our findings extend this link by showing a correspondence between neural processing in hMT+ and motion discrimination performance in human subjects.
evidence: This is a summary of the contribution of the current study.

claim: Strong suppression of fMRI responses was observed in EVC at both low and high stimulus contrast.
source: While neural processing in hMT+ seemed more closely linked to perception, strong suppression of fMRI responses was observed in EVC at both low and high stimulus contrast (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in the fMRI data from EVC in Figure 3B.

claim: Feed-forward and feedback connections between EVC and MT are thought to play an important role in spatial context processing.
source: Feed-forward and feedback connections between EVC and MT are thought to play an important role in spatial context processing (Angelucci and Bressloff, 2006)
evidence: This is established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: The data alone are not sufficient to determine the extent to which MT inherits suppression from EVC and/or drives this suppression via feedback.
source: our data alone are not sufficient to determine the extent to which MT inherits suppression from EVC and/or drives this suppression via feedback.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Surround suppression in early visual areas is well established in animal models.
source: However, surround suppression in early visual areas (e.g. V1, V2) is well established in animal models (Angelucci and Bressloff, 2006)
evidence: This is established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Suppressed fMRI responses in early visual areas generally correspond with perceptual suppression during contrast judgments.
source: and suppressed fMRI responses in these areas generally correspond with perceptual suppression during contrast judgments (Zenger-Landolt and Heeger, 2003; Schallmo et al., 2016; Joo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human fMRI studies.

claim: Some amount of spatial suppression during motion discrimination may be attributed to neural suppression in EVC.
source: This raises the possibility that some amount of spatial suppression during motion discrimination may be attributed to neural suppression in EVC.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of strong suppression in EVC.

claim: Other aspects of motion processing in MT are believed to be inherited from earlier stages of visual processing.
source: Other aspects of motion processing in MT are also believed to be inherited from earlier stages of visual processing (Kohn and Movshon, 2003; Glasser et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: One issue for comparing fMRI results between hMT+ and EVC is the difference in RF sizes between areas.
source: One issue for comparing fMRI results between hMT+ and EVC is the difference in RF sizes between areas.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration discussed by the authors.

claim: Neurons in foveal MT are thought to have a RF diameter of ~5°.
source: Neurons in foveal MT are thought to have a RF diameter of ~5°, while RFs in foveal EVC are much smaller (~1–2° diameter, depending on the visual area) (Raiguel et al., 1995; Liu et al., 2016; Tadin et al., 2003; Amano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about receptive field sizes, supported by citations.

claim: The largest stimuli are expected to extend into the extra-classical RF surround for foveal neurons in both hMT+ and EVC.
source: Our largest stimuli (12° diameter) are therefore expected to extend into the extra-classical RF surround for foveal neurons in both areas.
evidence: This is inferred from the stimulus sizes and known receptive field sizes.

claim: The ability to measure spatial suppression and summation with fMRI is affected by RF size.
source: Our ability to measure spatial suppression and summation with fMRI will also be affected by RF size; larger RFs in MT should make these measurement more difficult, because of less retinotopic specificity within a given voxel (Amano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a methodological consideration, supported by citation.

claim: In about 80% of subjects, voxels within hMT+ were identified that responded selectively to foveal > surrounding stimuli.
source: However, in about 80% of subjects, we were able to identify voxels within hMT+ that responded selectively to foveal > surrounding stimuli.
evidence: This describes the success rate of the ROI identification procedure.

claim: The hMT+ sub-ROIs showed both spatial suppression and summation.
source: These hMT+ sub-ROIs showed both spatial suppression and summation (Figure 3), indicating that we have the necessary spatial specificity to observe these phenomena in hMT+ in general.
evidence: This is shown in the fMRI data in Figure 3.

claim: The fMRI responses to increasing stimulus size from voxels outside of the center-selective hMT+ sub-ROIs were very different and cannot be attributed primarily to spatial suppression or summation.
source: The fMRI responses to increasing stimulus size from voxels outside of the center-selective hMT+ sub-ROIs were very different (data not shown), and cannot be attributed primarily to spatial suppression or summation.
evidence: This is stated by the authors based on unreported data.

claim: Future work with higher spatial resolution imaging may provide greater insight into the nature of spatial suppression and summation within hMT+.
source: Future work with higher spatial resolution imaging may provide greater insight into the nature of spatial suppression and summation within hMT+.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.
